newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HENMAN SET FOR CHANG, GRAF TO PLAY ON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HENMAN SET FOR CHANG, GRAF TO PLAY ON.

text.p: Britain's Tim Henman blasted his way to a date with Michael Chang on Wednesday as Steffi Graf declared she would not allow her father's tax evasion trial to derail her bid for a fifth Australian Open title.

Henman, last year's darling of Wimbledon, served and volleyed his way to an impressive 6-3 6-3 6-4 victory over Frenchman Guillaume Raoux. He will meet Chang, a straight sets winner over American Richey Reneberg, in the third round.
Graf, the German top seed and world number one, survived a scare against Latvian doubles specialist Laris Neiland to win her second-round match.

But she vowed to carry on through the tournament even though her father, Peter Graf, faces a possible jail sentence for tax evasion if he is found guilty in a verdict expected hours before the women's final.
"I knew already when I came here when the ending of the trial would be and I am playing until I am done with this tournament," Graf said after beating Neiland 7-5 6-2.

Prosecutors have asked that Peter Graf serve six years and nine months in jail if convicted of tax evasion charges involving more than 19.2 million marks (US$12.19 million) of his daughter's tennis earnings between 1989 and 1993.
Back on court, though, interest is already mounting in Henman's meeting with Chang, a 6-3 7-5 6-1 winner over fellow American Richey Reneberg.

Second seed Chang and Spain's Carlos Moya, who has ousted champion Boris Becker and Patrick McEnroe in his first two matches, are leading the charge of the baseline brigade, but Chang may have to review his tactics against Henman who managed 11 aces against Raoux.
Henman, who last year became the first Briton to make the quarter-finals at Wimbledon in 23 years, is unseeded in Melbourne.
But he has soared to 14th in the world rankings after winning a pre-Open warm-up tournament in Sydney and said on Wednesday he planned to take the game to Chang.
"I feel that if I can be aggressive, then maybe I can be the dictator," he said.
Some of the harder hitters have complained that conditions at Melbourne Park this year are more favourable to baseliners than in past championships.

World number one Pete Sampras and Becker have complained about the softness of the tennis balls in use, claiming their slow speed through the air puts aggressive serve and volley players at a disadvantage.
Neither Chang nor Moya said they saw any difference in the balls from last year and the Spaniard suggested Becker's tirade might have been sour grapes.

"I feel good about these balls. Maybe it is better for the baseliners (but) the one who complained was Becker -- maybe because he lost," said Moya, a tall, long-haired 20-year-old who has become a favourite with the female fans in Melbourne.
Japan's Rika Hiraki caused the biggest upset of the day, ousting women's 10th seed Brenda Schultz-McCarthy 0-6 6-1 6-4.
Hiraki, 25, said she could not concentrate during the first set because she was not used to playing in front of a crowd, but she came back forcefully as Schultz-McCarthy lost her composure.
Another loser was 12th seed Magnus Gustafsson of Sweden, beaten 3-6 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-4 by German Karsten Braasch.

Former champion Mary Pierce of France, now on a comeback, celebrated her 22nd birthday with a 6-2 6-2 win over Natalia Medvedeva of Ukraine. Pierce ousted 13th seed Elena Likhovtseva in the first round.

The most exhausted winners of the day were Australians Jon Ireland and Wayne Arthurs, who entered the record book when they beat Italians Cristian Brandi and Filippo Messori. Their final set tally -- 29-27 -- was the highest in the event's known history.
